newsitem.title: UK: UK court rules against Customs & Excise on VAT.
newsitem.headline: UK court rules against Customs & Excise on VAT.

text.p: The British High Court ruled on Tuesday that Customs & Excise acted illegally when it refused to pay out on claims for back-dated indirect tax (VAT) extending beyond three years, sources close to the case said.
Since July 18, Customs has withheld payments on claims beyond three years and will now have to pay back VAT which companies overpaid.

"The Court found Custom's policy to delay payment was ultra vires and unlawful," said an adviser to some of the companies which brought the case. "It said there was nothing in the VAT law that gave (Customs) the power to defer payment."
A Customs & Excise spokesman said it estimated the cost of the repayments for the High Court cases and other similar cases pending was around 35 million stg.
The actions were brought by a number of parties including the Federation of Ophthalmic and Dispensing Opticians, mail order group Great Universal Stores and the National Provident Institution.
However if the three-year limit on repayments becomes law as expected in December, Customs said it will be able to claw back any cash it has been forced to pay out.
The government announced on July 18 this year that it was planning to present the three-year limit in a bill to Parliament as part of the November 26 budget.

The Customs spokesman said the High Court ruling did not mean the three year cap was illegal, merely its decision to withhold payment. "When the law is passed, hopefully in December, we will claw any money back," he said.
But many companies plan to continue their fight against the three-year limit, even if it is passed in December, and have formed The Refunds Action Group to lobby ministers and Members of Parliament.
Customs & Excise may have to pay out on another series of cases on VAT.

On October 24, it lost a case at the European Court on back payments of VAT on discounted goods. That will cost it 70 million on Customs' calculations, and up to 200 million stg if the three year limit fails to become law.

Other cases, including a major one on interest-free credit deals, could cost Customs up to 5.0 billion stg. This case is due to be heard soon by the House of Lords which is expected to find in favour of Customs.
